source.title: Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models
source.authors: Leonardo Defilippis; Florent Krzakala; Bruno Loureiro; A. Maillard

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and reports scaling results in a new setting: synthetic hierarchical multi-index supervised learning with shallow neural networks, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as background, but does not test language-model pretraining loss, extrapolation from small language-model runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or downstream task predictability from pretraining loss. Its own results bear on V5 through scaling in a non-language supervised setting. The individual-feature recovery threshold is a related scaling result not directly named by a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and partly simulates power-law error scaling in sample size for a non-language setting: synthetic hierarchical multi-index regression learned by Bayes, spectral and two-layer-network estimators. That bears on V5 only, as a toy theoretical setting. It has no language-model pretraining, no parameter or compute scaling, and no allocation, architecture or downstream results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also stress universality: the rates match earlier quadratic-network results and LASSO minimax rates. They present a solvable setting where scaling laws and progressive feature emergence arise together.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies theoretical Bayes and spectral recovery rates and supervised two-layer-network training on synthetic hierarchical targets, rather than language-model pretraining sweeps over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The rates depend on hierarchy exponent γ and on the sample-complexity regime relative to m⋆; the neural-network result also specifies the activation, width, and regularization conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Features are recovered sequentially: the kth direction becomes detectable at α≈k^(2γ) (Figure 2 spikes), giving a cascade of phase transitions with plateaus and drops in error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Error scaling in hierarchical tasks arises from sequential feature emergence at index-dependent sample thresholds.

record.problems: The results rely on isotropic Gaussian covariates, two-layer architectures, and an asymptotic high-dimensional analysis. The authors note that attaining the rates with SGD without spectral initialization or explicit regularization remains open. The finite-size experiment described for Figure 1 is averaged over 70 instances, with no uncertainty estimates stated.

untested.parts: Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. Scaling in model size or compute (width p does not enter the rates). Networks trained end-to-end by SGD/GD, which the authors leave open. Any empirical large-scale system.
Untested: no extrapolation from fitted small runs.
Untested: no shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Untested: no comparison of fitting or setup choices for language-model laws.

record.verdict_notes: This is a purely theoretical toy-model paper, plus one small simulation. The scaling variable is sample size (α=n/d); the target complexity m⋆ is not model size. Its bearing on V5 is weak and indirect, so researchers should weigh the verdicts accordingly. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger language-model runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including the relative growth rates of parameters and data.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architectures at fixed parameter count.
The study tests scaling in synthetic hierarchical supervised learning, not image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from language-model pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations on counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

conditions.value: g(z) = tanh(z²) − [tanh(z²)]; g(z) = |z| − √(2/π); g(z) = 1/12 He₂(z) + 2·1/4! He₄(z)

rows.value: The text reports a crossover around α ≍ m⋆^(2γ) ≈ 400 between rates α^(−1+1/(2γ)) and m⋆/α.
rows.note: The reported crossover is described for the displayed experiments averaged over 70 instances; the text does not give separate numerical values for each target variant.
rows.check: The evidence is qualitative from Figure 1: a crossover between two exponents near α≈400, at d=1000, m⋆=10, γ=1.3. No fitted exponents or uncertainty are given. It shows a change of slope, not a single power law.

source_check.correct: The polynomial target is g(z) = (1/2)He₂(z) + [1/(2·4!)]He₄(z). The reported crossover is α ≍ m⋆^(2γ) ≈ 400, between α^(−1+1/(2γ)) and m⋆/α.

relationships.condition: Synthetic scale-free hierarchical multi-index regression, γ>1/2 or data-rich regime; Bayes, spectral estimator, and two-layer network with spectral init plus ridge readout
relationships.reason: Error falls as a power law in sample complexity: α^(−1+1/(2γ)) or m⋆/α (R1, R2, R4). The spectral and network procedures match these rates (R5, R6), and finite-size runs show the predicted behaviour (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Error scaled as α^(−1+1/(2γ)) or m⋆/α, with spectral and network procedures matching these rates and finite-size experiments recovering the predicted behavior.

relationships.condition: γ<1/2 with α≪m⋆; and across the α≈m⋆^(2γ) crossover
relationships.reason: In this regime error plateaus at Θ(1) with no power-law decrease (R3). Elsewhere the exponent switches between regimes rather than following one power law (R1, R2, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Error remained Θ(1) without power-law improvement in the plateau regime, while scaling exponents changed across the crossover.

tranche.reason: The paper derives and simulates sample-scaling laws in a new setting: hierarchical multi-index regression with Bayes, spectral, and two-stage neural-network estimators.

source_check.notes: The results concern feature-recovery error and two-stage network excess risk; Remark 3.9 does not establish the Bayes-optimal prediction-risk rate. End-to-end SGD attainment remains open; Remark 3.5 supplies a first-layer GD interpretation of the spectral method.
